What actually gets you into the UN?
It’s not what most people think.

After decades in the UN system, including serving at senior levels, I have seen thousands of CVs cross my desk.

One pattern appeared again and again:
	👉 The candidates who succeeded rarely had “perfect” profiles.
	👉 They had substance.

What does substance mean in practice?

• Languages
English or French remain essential for many positions. Additional languages such as Spanish, Arabic, or others can significantly expand opportunities. Multilingual professionals have advantages.

• Technical expertise
Strong knowledge in a specific field:
governance, economics, public health, climate, women’s empowerment, humanitarian response, crisis management, development projects, HR, procurement, finance, data, digital systems, but also political affairs, disarmament, among others.

The UN increasingly looks for people with identifiable expertise, not generic international profiles.

• Field experience
Experience working with governments, communities, in crisis settings, or regular development operations matters enormously.
Field exposure develops judgment that cannot easily be taught in classrooms.

• Analytical capacity
The ability to synthesize complexity, identify risks, and present practical options to decision-makers.
This is tested constantly in UN work (and in interviews).

• Professional maturity
Understanding how institutions function:
	processes,
	political sensitivities,
	multicultural environments,
	intergovernmental dynamics,
	and the importance of balance and diplomacy under pressure.

• Writing ability
Clear, concise communication that works across cultures and audiences.

What matters less than many people assume:

	• Prestigious university names
	• “UN-focused” master’s degrees
	• Social media visibility
	• Paid career coaching
	• Constant networking performance

The UN recruits professionals who can already show they can contribute effectively in complex institutional environments.

And one important point that younger professionals sometimes overlook:

👉 The best preparation for a UN career is often building genuine expertise outside the UN first. 

In governments, NGOs, research institutions, humanitarian organizations, national administrations, municipalities, regional organizations, or private-sector technical work.

These are not merely stepping stones.
They are often where professional credibility is actually built.

I joined the UN only after years of experience in government, consultancy, academia, and an international development bank.

The UN recruits professionals who can already demonstrate they are able to contribute effectively in complex institutional environments.

The strongest candidates focused on becoming excellent professionals first, not on “getting into the UN”.

What skills are you building today?

There is a lot of discussion about green hydrogen. But the real question is about development impact.
 
Green hydrogen has the potential to decarbonise hard-to-electrify sectors, support green industrialisation, create jobs, and strengthen energy security. Often described as the fuel of the future, it is projected to supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050.
 
But that future is not guaranteed.
 
Green hydrogen also places significant pressure on land, water, and energy systems. Producing 1 million tonnes of hydrogen requires around 30,000 hectares of solar panels, while nearly 70% of planned electrolyser capacity is located in water-stressed regions.
 
Three takeaways stand out:
🔹 Green hydrogen is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Countries must weigh water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.
 
🔹 Hydrogen must create domestic value. India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 500,000 jobs and 125 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, backed by $1.83 billion for domestic electrolyser manufacturing.
 
🔹 Inclusion must be designed from the start. By 2023, although 4.3 GW of green hydrogen capacity had been announced globally, only 0.3 GW, around 7%, had actually been built. The challenge is increasingly about planning, institutions, and governance.
 
Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not only markets. The opportunities are real, but only if local communities, institutions, and the private sector are included from day one.
 
I look forward to discussing these questions further at today’s panel discussion, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework, at the University of Oxford .
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustEnergyTransition TIDE Centre, University of Oxford

The small vial in front of George contains the entire contents of the 236-page book he's resting his paw against. But it's not a flash drive or other type of off-the-shelf storage. If green hydrogen is the future, who gets to own that future?

By 2050, hydrogen is projected to supply around 12% of global energy demand, with demand rising to over 430 million tonnes. Yet around 83% of global hydrogen investment remains concentrated in Europe and China, even as many of the world's most competitive low-cost production sites are likely to emerge across Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

This raises a bigger development question: will countries become producers of green hydrogen, or creators of the industries, jobs, and value chains built around it?

This was a central theme from today's discussion at the University of Oxford on the UNDP  -TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  report Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework.

While the opportunity is growing rapidly, delivery is still struggling to keep pace. By 2023, although 4.3 GW of global green hydrogen capacity had been announced, only 0.3 GW — around 7% — had actually been built. The constraint is no longer renewable potential alone. Increasingly, the barriers are governance, finance, infrastructure, and institutional readiness.

Three strategic priorities stand out:

🔹 From export commodities to integrated value chains. Hydrogen should be viewed not only as an export opportunity, but as an industrial strategy. The greatest development gains may come from local manufacturing, green fertilisers, and decarbonised industries — not raw hydrogen exports.

🔹 Jobs, skills, and national innovation systems. Chile aims to create over 100,000 jobs through its hydrogen strategy, while India targets around 500,000 jobs and 125 GW of renewable capacity by 2030. South Korea shows how coordinated ecosystems across research institutions, universities, and industry can transform hydrogen into a national innovation system.

🔹 Linking hydrogen finance and infrastructure with public value. The risk is that hydrogen projects become closed export enclaves — privately powered, externally financed, and weakly connected to domestic economies. South Africa's hydrogen strategy includes EU support for ports, railways, and pipeline infrastructure, while Brazil's Ceará Green Hydrogen Hub is anchoring around $7 billion in industrial and logistics investments.

The success of green hydrogen will not be measured by megawatts or export contracts alone. It will be measured by whether countries build capabilities, create decent jobs, safeguard resources, and advance shared prosperity.

The energy transition must, above all, serve people.

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustEnergyTransition

Sustainable and inclusive energy access is a literal catalyst to all 1️⃣7️⃣ SDGs. But how can we make it happen? We're proposing a holistic and systems-level approach to leveraging tech to drive a just energy transition. We call it the 'Digital Energy Stack' ⬇️

The ‘digital energy stack’ is 7️⃣ tech (and non-tech) components that countries need to engage with to maximise the benefits of the AI, digital, and energy revolutions. 

📊 Data: the fuel of the energy revolution. From the Big Data generated by smart meters to the ‘Thick’ Data that needs to inform service design and policymaking.

📱 Connectivity: the wired and wireless infrastructure that lets data flow between energy solutions and stakeholders – and drives energy business models. 

🌐 Compute: the ‘currency’ of the 21st century - creating opportunities for improved energy planning and delivery, but also challenges of energy and resource use.

🛣️ Digital Public Infrastructure: the ‘roads and railways’ of our digital economies and societies, DPI could deepen the impact of digital energy solutions. 

🔒 Cybersecurity: energy is critical national infrastructure. It needs to be ‘resilient-by-design’ and we need energy professionals with cyber skills.

🤖 AI: already having an impact - whether in improving energy planning or driving new approaches for credit-scoring that make energy services more accessible.

🏛️ Governance: how we shape the skills, expertise, processes, institutions, and organisational cultures – within and beyond government – to truly engage with the potential that digital offers for energy.

Can AI in energy systems become a development opportunity, or will it deepen existing divides?

AI-enabled forecasting and optimization could unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity from existing power lines, without building a single new one. Improved forecasting has already increased wind power market value by up to 20% in some systems, while AI-driven fault detection can reduce outage durations by 30 to 50%.

But the stakes are equally high. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households, while more than 2,500 GW of renewable, storage, and large-load projects remain stuck in grid queues globally. The story can go one of two ways. If we are not careful, AI can push energy systems beyond what people and the planet can sustain. If we are deliberate, it can strengthen resilience and fairness.

This is what I will be exploring today at the University of Cambridge in a lecture titled "What Will Your Knowledge Make Possible?" with the next generation of energy leaders, looking at how energy, digital systems, and AI are converging into what I call planetary intelligence, and three priorities that stand out:

🔹 Treat energy data as public infrastructure to unlock investment at scale. Shared intelligence on demand, grid capacity, and system performance can reduce uncertainty and accelerate investment.
🔹 Govern AI and energy within land, water, and social limits. AI infrastructure cannot be planned outside ecological realities and resource constraints.
🔹 Measure success by access, resilience, and opportunity for people. The value of energy intelligence is ultimately measured through jobs, services, and human outcomes.

The future of energy is not something we simply predict. It is something we collectively build. Looking forward to today's conversation in #Cambridge University and to hearing perspectives from the next generation helping shape what comes next.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #AI

What kind of future do you envision in this new era of energy transition and digital revolution?
 
Today at the University of Cambridge, I had the pleasure of discussing how artificial intelligence, energy systems, and digital infrastructure are increasingly converging into the same transformation, reshaping economies, industrial systems, and development pathways simultaneously.
 
Throughout history, major energy transitions changed far more than how societies generated power.
 
And now we may be entering a new inflection point: planetary intelligence - the emergence of an intelligent layer across energy systems, digital infrastructure, finance, satellites, sensors, and public institutions.
 
Artificial intelligence is often described as something virtual. Yet it is becoming deeply physical. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households.
 
But perhaps the deeper question is this: Do we know yet whether AI will reduce inequality or deepen it?
 
The answer is, we do not know yet. What we do know is that behind every major technological shift lies a transformational opportunity.
 
Three opportunities particularly stood out during today’s discussion:
 
• Build AI infrastructure that strengthens energy systems rather than fragmenting them. Across Africa, data-centre demand could grow from around 0.4 GW today to between 1.5 and 2.2 GW by 2030, requiring an estimated $10–20 billion in investment. If planned strategically, this growth could help accelerate grid modernization, renewable integration, energy efficiency, and resilient infrastructure development.
 
• Turn renewable energy systems into intelligent systems. Renewable systems are becoming too large, decentralized, and dynamic to manage without advanced coordination. AI-enabled transmission management alone could unlock up to 175 GW of additional grid capacity from existing infrastructure.
 
• Build national digital-energy ecosystems and local value chains. Around $5.8 trillion is expected to flow into global grid infrastructure between 2026 and 2035, including roughly $700 billion in digital grid technologies. The deeper opportunity lies in building local industries, technical capabilities, services, software ecosystems, and new value chains around the transition itself.
 
Perhaps this is ultimately why the AI-energy transition matters for development.
 
Because energy innovation is never only about producing electricity differently. It is about reshaping how societies manage water, food systems, cities, industry, health, jobs, and resilience.
 
Many thanks to the University of Cambridge and all students for the engaging discussion today.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment

What does a just energy transition really look like in practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In a school in Banja Luka, energy efficiency renovations have cut energy use by nearly half — making classrooms warmer, brighter, and easier to maintain for more than a thousand students and staff. Small changes like these signal a deeper transformation underway across the country.

In a new op-ed, "A Shared Just Energy Transition," I share why this transition is not only an energy shift, but one of the largest shared development opportunities for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Three priorities stand out:
🔹 Strengthen governance to unlock finance in renewables. Bosnia and Herzegovina's transition will require over $6 billion in investment, with the grid at the centre. With the Electricity Law and the National Energy and Climate Plan in their final stage of approval, the foundations are in place to mobilize bankable pipelines and innovative financing.

🔹 Transform coal regions into jobs, skills, and growth. Coal still employs 15,000 to 20,000 people directly and supports more than 150,000 jobs across related sectors. Repurposing mine land in Zenica, Banovići, and Kreka — with around 27 MWp of solar capacity planned — shows how existing infrastructure can be turned into productive economic assets when connected to a national innovation ecosystem.

🔹 Harness data, AI, and digital innovation to scale energy efficiency. Public buildings retrofitted through UNDP's Green Economic Development programme have already reduced energy use by 30 to 50 percent. With smart meter deployment already exceeding the 80% national target, accelerating their full use can unlock real-time data, dynamic tariffs, and stronger system resilience.

As UNDP , we stand ready to support this whole-of-system transformation by helping connect policy, finance, and technology to build resilience, create jobs, improve quality of life, and position Bosnia and Herzegovina at the forefront of the next generation of energy innovation.

🔗 More on UNDP's work in Bosnia and Herzegovina: https://lnkd.in/eSxRHd5B

On Saturday, I joined the 2026 Oxford Africa Conference  Conference panel, “Powering Africa’s Energy Futures: From Resources to Markets.”
What stayed with me most was the urgency of reframing Africa’s energy transition as a development agenda, but, at the same time, the incredible opportunities the continent holds.
 
Around 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still lack access to electricity, and more than 940 million people remain without clean cooking. The question is how energy systems can power homes, schools, hospitals, and businesses today, while also building the foundations for tomorrow’s industries, digital infrastructure, and AI economy.
 
This is where AI becomes central. Africa’s AI future will be shaped by its energy choices. Data centres, cloud systems, cooling infrastructure, and compute capacity all require reliable power. Africa’s data-centre capacity could grow from around 400 MW today to as much as 2.2 GW by 2030, yet the continent still receives only around 2% of global clean energy investment.
 
That gap is technical, financial, and political. Closing it will require affordable capital, stronger delivery systems, investable pipelines, and institutions capable of turning ambition into implementation.
 
But the opportunity goes far beyond electricity access. Africa holds around 30% of the world’s known mineral reserves and renewable energy potential estimated at 1,000 times projected electricity demand in 2040. The challenge is whether the continent remains a supplier of raw materials, or builds value chains in renewables, batteries, e-mobility, digital infrastructure, and AI-enabled systems.
Africa’s energy transition could create 26 million additional jobs by 2050, including more than 8 million in renewables. Reliable clean energy now underpins not only climate action, but also competitiveness, industrialisation, jobs, and economic sovereignty.

I had a great conversation last week with students from the Cambridge African Studies and Energy Society on Africa’s energy future, green industrialization, and the role young people are already playing in shaping it. 
 
Three reflections stayed with me from today’s discussion: 

	1.	Africa’s energy transition is about far more than electricity generation. It is fundamentally about development, jobs, digital transformation, and expanding opportunity across the continent. Yet while Africa holds around 30% of the world’s critical mineral deposits, 565 million people still lack access to electricity. 
 
	2.	Young people are already driving change. In 2023, climate tech startups accounted for 36% of Africa’s startup market, attracting around $1.1 billion in investment. From AI-enabled energy systems to clean energy entrepreneurship, many of the systems of tomorrow are already being shaped today. 
 
	3.	The transition must also be equitable. Around 10–12 million young Africans enter the labor market each year, while only around 3 million formal jobs are created annually. Expanding local value creation, regional cooperation, and access to affordable finance will be essential to ensuring the energy transition translates into long-term economic opportunity. 

What gave me the most hope was hearing students speak openly about their goals, concerns, and visions for the future, and the deep desire many share to contribute meaningfully to their communities and countries. 
 
One thing I shared with them is something I continue reminding myself of as well: meaningful careers rarely follow a straight line. Real change is often built gradually, through persistence, curiosity, collaboration, and the willingness to keep moving forward despite uncertainty. 
 
Thank you again to everyone who made the discussion so thoughtful and inspiring.

What frontiers are #SIDS 🏝️ leading in when it comes to sustainable energy innovation?
 
Is it about
🌱 Vertical and urban farming, where food production depends on energy in places with less than 1% arable land
🏝️ Tourism economies generating 20 to 70% of GDP, yet losing value through diesel at 1 to 2 dollars per litre
🚤 E-mobility and marine transport reshaping connectivity, trade, and fisheries
🏙️ Digital islands, with urban centers growing around 4% annually as new economic hubs
🌊 Coastal adaptation, where erosion, flooding, and infrastructure risks require energy and spatial planning together
 
At the Pacific SIDS Regional Energy Symposium in Port Moresby, I reflected on how sustainable energy is not only driving an energy transition, but shaping a new model for development in SIDS.
 
What is emerging across SIDS:
 
1. Geospatial and AI-driven planning: With platforms like Digital Earth Pacific mapping over 34,000 kilometers of coastline, countries can identify risks and prioritize investments with far greater precision. Through the SIDS Data Platform, UNDP supports this with more than 4,000 indicators and 80 geospatial datasets.
 
2. Energy-linked whole island value chains: In Tonga, solar-powered mini-factories produce around 260,000 litres of coconut products annually. In Samoa, clean energy is extending into transport and fisheries, supported by low-carbon marine engines and more than 80 EV charging stations.
 
3. Financing distributed energy at scale: Under UNDP’s Pacific Green Transformation Project, supported by the Government of Japan, a 1 megawatt solar farm in Buin is reducing electricity costs by up to 50%, strengthening energy security, and benefiting more than 30,000 people.
 
UNDP, working across the Pacific, Caribbean, and AIS regions, is supporting this transformation through the “Rising Up for SIDS” Energy Offer, developed with AOSIS and rapidly operationalized following the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda.

With the 6th Pacific Regional Energy and Transport Ministers’ Meeting next week and pre-COP preparations ahead of #COP31 , the task is clear: scale progress faster with the partnerships, finance, and tools to match SIDS’ ambition.

If you are working in this space, please reach out to us. As UNDP , we are ready to partner and support. #EnergyForDevelopment #RisingUpForSIDS

Everyone is talking about the AI 'race'. But races aren't won in the first corner. They're won in the final sprint - and over the very last mile. And the last mile is something that the Global South knows very well.

Far from being left out or left behind, the Global South could set the pace for global AI direction. And we're working with governments around the world to prepare them for what we see as the crucial AI 'sprint' - in particular, how countries can position energy and AI as crucial catalysts for growth. With these two revolutions having the potential to become definitive inflection points for 21st century sustainable development. 

We've identified a 'Green Window of Opportunity' where decision-makers, policymakers, and innovators can leverage the combined potential of energy and AI to chart a new pathway. Some of the areas we're driving exploration around include:

🤝 How to build locally-owned and locally-relevant domestic AI–energy innovation ecosystems anchored in local talent, universities, businesses, and public institutions.

🏛️ The need to make 'Green AI' THE critical pathway through supportive regulation, infrastructure planning, and investment incentives - with the potential for this to become an area of national comparative advantage.

⬆️ Identifying how countries and communities can move up the clean energy, critical mineral, and digital value chains to retain greater economic value domestically - and how they can build crucial and cumulative energy, AI, and development gains.

⚡ How countries can shape and support AI and clean-energy entrepreneurs through targeted finance, incubation, market creation, and skills development.

We are not about abstract discussions of technology, status quo energy policy, or generic policy recommendations. We really do see an important moment for development in the coming months and years. Countries sitting at the intersection of renewable energy - many of which are in the Global South - and AI explorations (with countries across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific moving quickly) could reap an unprecedented digital development dividend. Get in touch if you want to explore what the AI and energy revolutions could mean for your country.

Can we move from Artificial Intelligence to Planetary Intelligence?

As we mark World Environment Day, this may be one of the most important questions of our time.
When World Environment Day was established in 1973, it carried the slogan "Only One Earth." More than 50 years later, that message feels more relevant than ever.

Today, the world is navigating profound transformations. Rising geopolitical tensions are reshaping energy security, while rapid advances in digitalization and artificial intelligence are accelerating demand for electricity and critical resources.
 
Yet amid these challenges, there are reasons for optimism. Despite the impacts of conflicts in the Middle East, global energy investment is expected to increase by 5%, reaching USD 3.4 trillion in 2026.
 
2025 also marked a historic milestone: for the first time, renewable energy generated more electricity globally than coal. Solar power expanded more rapidly in 2025 than any energy source in history.
 
The opportunity is significant. A just energy transition could reduce energy import bills by 38%, create 14 million green jobs, and lift 45 million people out of energy poverty by 2035.
 
At the same time, data centres already account for around 2% of global electricity demand and are projected to more than double their consumption by 2030. Yet the same technologies driving this growth can become part of the solution. AI-enabled grid management and digital twins are already improving renewable energy integration by 20–30%, helping build more flexible and efficient energy systems. More than half of critical mineral projects overlap with or are located near Indigenous Peoples' lands. 
 
But intelligence alone is not enough. The challenge is how we apply it.
 
Planetary Intelligence means using innovation not only to optimize economies, but also to better understand and manage the interconnected relationship between energy, nature, communities, and development. It means recognizing that healthy ecosystems, forests, wetlands, and oceans are as critical to our future as data centres, grids, and digital infrastructure. Nature-based solutions alone could provide up to one-third of the climate mitigation needed by 2030 while strengthening resilience and protecting livelihoods.
 
There is only one Earth. If we choose the right path, the journey from Artificial Intelligence to Planetary Intelligence may become one of the defining opportunities of our generation.

G7 leaders are gathering in Évian today to discuss energy security, AI, and critical minerals.
 
One question stays with me: Can countries make the right development choices before infrastructure is locked in?
 
I have come to see energy modelling not as a technical exercise, but as a way to inform decisions before they become irreversible. Without integrated planning, countries risk fuel import dependence, grid congestion, stranded assets, and missed jobs. With it, energy systems can be designed for industrialization, resilience, and inclusive growth from the start.
 
Three takeaways stand out:
 
🔹 Model demand and risk at subnational scale.
With more than 1,000 active Earth observation satellites, a tenfold rise in publicly available Earth observation data in a decade, and over 500 machine-learning-ready geospatial datasets, governments can now model demand growth, climate risk, and system constraints below the national level. That means infrastructure can go where it is most resilient, affordable, and impactful.
 
🔹 Link energy decisions to real development outcomes.
The transition is full of trade-offs: cost and resilience, speed and equity, access and industrial growth. Integrated models help countries test scenarios side by side, asking not only what is cheapest, but what is most robust under climate shocks, what reduces fuel imports, and what creates the most jobs per dollar invested. Complexity becomes a set of choices governments can act on.
 
🔹 Align governments and finance around one evidence base.
When planning ministries, utilities, finance ministries, and regulators work from the same models, coordination improves. Pipelines become clearer. Policy becomes more coherent. Finance becomes easier to mobilize. Modelling becomes a common language linking national plans, climate commitments, and investment decisions into one credible framework.
 
The conversations in Évian will shape the global energy agenda. But the deeper test is whether every country, not only the G7, can shape its own future with the same foresight. 
 
Energy modelling is no longer an add-on. It is strategic infrastructure. And it decides whether a country locks in vulnerability or builds lasting resilience.

Contributing to the review of this year’s Tracking SDG7 Progress Report through the SDG7 Youth Constituency of the Major Group for Children and Youth made one thing impossible to ignore:

2️⃣ Clean cooking must sit at the centre of SDG7 delivery. Around 2.0 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. Without a course correction, 1.8 billion people could still lack clean cooking access by 2030.

3️⃣ Finance must reach where energy poverty is concentrated. Public clean energy flows reached at least USD 24.6 billion in 2024, but flows to LDCs fell by 11%. LDCs, LLDCs and SIDS collectively received less than 30% of public clean energy finance, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the global population without electricity access.

These aren’t just access gaps. They’re development gaps; shaping whether people can study, work, access healthcare, build businesses and live with dignity.

What’s missing isn’t technology. It’s the urgency, coordination and political will to match commitments with resources AND to make sure progress translates into delivery on the ground.

Ahead of next week's High-Level Political Forum, the latest Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report offers an important snapshot of where the global energy transition stands—and why this may be one of the greatest development opportunities of our time.
 
The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.
Today, investing in clean energy is no longer driven only by climate ambition. It is increasingly about energy security, economic competitiveness, industrial development and resilience.
 
At the same time, digitalization and AI are creating new opportunities to build smarter grids, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewables and expand access to affordable and reliable energy.
 
Accelerating renewable energy deployment and energy efficiency strengthens energy security, reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and enhances macroeconomic resilience, particularly in developing countries.
Important gaps remain. 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030, nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels, and globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford a basic electricity connection.
 
Universal access will require us to more than triple the current pace of progress.
 
As the final in-depth review of SDG 7 before 2030, this year's High-Level Political Forum is an opportunity not only to assess progress, but to redefine the just energy transition as one of the strongest drivers of development, resilience, prosperity and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.

Ahead of next week's High-Level Political Forum, the latest Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report offers an important snapshot of where the global energy transition stands—and why this may be one of the greatest development opportunities of our time.
 
The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.
Today, investing in clean energy is no longer driven only by climate ambition. It is increasingly about energy security, economic competitiveness, industrial development and resilience.
 
At the same time, digitalization and AI are creating new opportunities to build smarter grids, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewables and expand access to affordable and reliable energy.
 
Accelerating renewable energy deployment and energy efficiency strengthens energy security, reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and enhances macroeconomic resilience, particularly in developing countries.
Important gaps remain. 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030, nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels, and globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford a basic electricity connection.
 
Universal access will require us to more than triple the current pace of progress.
 
As the final in-depth review of SDG 7 before 2030, this year's High-Level Political Forum is an opportunity not only to assess progress, but to redefine the just energy transition as one of the strongest drivers of development, resilience, prosperity and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.

What if SDG 7 is not only about closing the access gap, but about building clean, affordable energy systems that power the next generation of development?
 
That was the question I kept coming back to today while moderating Panel Discussion 3: Accelerating Progress Towards 2030 and Beyond during the webinar “Clean and Affordable Energy: Where do we stand? How to move forward?”, ahead of the SDG 7 review at the HLPF.
 
There is real momentum to build on. For the first time in history, universal electricity access is within reach. More than 90% of the global population now has access to basic electricity, and global investment in the energy transition reached a record US$2.3 trillion in 2025.
 
But the task ahead is changing. Geopolitical tensions are exposing the vulnerability of major energy routes, affecting around 20 million barrels of oil per day. AI and digitalisation are also increasing demand on energy systems. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than all but five countries, and enough water to meet the basic needs of 1.3 billion people in sub-Saharan Africa for a year.
 
The opportunity is to power digital transformation with clean, affordable and resilient energy systems while advancing a just energy transition for all.
 
I was joined by Divya Kottadiel from Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , @Luis Manuera from UN Environment Programme , and Isaac Elizondo  from UNIDO  for a rich exchange on what acceleration must look like in practice.
 
For me, one message stood out clearly: access must move from connection alone to energy for development and opportunity. That means powering schools, hospitals, farms, digital services and livelihoods, while creating jobs, supporting local enterprises and closing the digital divide for the 2.2 billion people still offline.
 
Finance is central to making this possible. Global clean energy investment has reached around US$2 trillion annually, yet Africa attracts only US$30-40 billion, roughly 2% of global flows. Redirecting capital toward countries and communities with the greatest needs is one of the biggest opportunities for shared prosperity.
 
If we get SDG 7 right, we do more than expand access. We make energy cleaner, more affordable and more productive, strengthening resilience, enabling digital participation, jobs and a just transition.

Solar is one of the fastest ways to expand electricity access, particularly in hard-to-reach rural communities. But with many systems such as solar inverters having a lifespan of 15-20 years, how do we ensure that today's clean energy solutions don't become tomorrow's sustainability challenge?
 
That question is becoming increasingly urgent as Africa's clean energy transition gains pace.
Installed renewable energy capacity has doubled over the past decade, from around 35 GW in 2015 to 70 GW in 2024, while 2025 recorded a record 11.3 GW of new renewable capacity additions, led by Ethiopia, South Africa and Egypt. Today, eight African countries generate more than 80% of their electricity from renewable sources.
 
As this momentum continues, the next challenge is ensuring these gains are built to last. Embedding circularity across renewable energy value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repurposing and second-life battery applications, can strengthen energy security, reduce waste, as well as create local industries and jobs.
 
Coming just days after the African Circular Economy Alliance Annual Meeting in Abidjan, I look forward to continuing this important conversation in New York at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa.
 
Circular energy systems aren't a separate conversation from our global energy systems. They are how we make the clean energy transition more resilient, more sustainable, and more beneficial for communities across Africa, and across the world.

What happens when the clean energy technologies we deploy today reach the end of their lives?
 
By 2050, the world could generate up to 78 million tonnes of retired solar panels. Recycling energy transition minerals could reduce the need for new mining by 25-40%, while creating a $200 billion global market. Yet circularity remains an overlooked—and key—part of the energy transition.
 
Today, I had the privilege of delivering the opening remarks and keynote at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa, alongside colleagues and partners from across the public and private sectors.
 
Circularity isn't just about managing waste. It's about designing energy systems from the start to maximize the value of every clean energy investment.
 
Three takeaways stood out:
•⁠  ⁠Circularity is an industrial opportunity. Repair, remanufacturing, recycling, and second-life applications can create jobs, strengthen local industries, and capture more value from the energy transition.
•⁠  ⁠Digitalization is an enabler. From battery passports and AI-assisted mineral discovery to smart grids that could reduce the continent's estimated $5 billion in annual transmission and distribution losses, data is becoming the backbone of circular energy systems.
•⁠  ⁠Regional cooperation is essential. Integrated regional value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repair, second-life use, and recycling, will be key to scaling circular industries.

As renewable and off-grid solar continue to expand across Africa, we have an opportunity to build energy systems that are circular, resilient, and designed to deliver long-term development benefits.
 
Thank you to all the organizers, speakers, and participants for an engaging discussion.

Honoured to be recognized by illuminem as one of the Top 10 Most Read Thought Leaders of the Year in AI.

This recognition feels especially meaningful at a moment when AI is reshaping how we think about energy, development, and sustainability. The question is no longer only how fast AI advances, but how responsibly it is powered, governed, and used to support a just energy transition.

At its foundation, the future of AI is a question of energy. Last year, AI consumed around 415 terawatt hours of electricity, more than 150 countries individually. By 2030, electricity demand from data centres is projected to more than double to around 945 terawatt hours, roughly equivalent to Japan’s entire electricity consumption today.

I have come to see this as less a story about technology than about people: whether the systems we build expand opportunity, strengthen resilience, and reach the communities that need them most. That question is not abstract when 655 million people still live without electricity and 2.0 billion people still lack access to clean cooking, even as AI places a vast new demand on the same energy systems.

The encouraging part is that AI also presents enormous opportunities to accelerate a just energy transition, from strengthening energy systems to expanding clean energy access. The challenge is ensuring these benefits are shared. Of the US$15.7 trillion AI is projected to contribute to the global economy by 2030, around 84% is expected to accrue to just three regions. A just transition means deliberately widening that circle, ensuring that the communities too often left behind are not left behind again.

At UNDP, we are working to ensure that emerging technologies accelerate clean energy access, strengthen resilience, and deliver real development outcomes for those who need them most.

Thank you to @illuminem and its global community of readers for this recognition. It is an honour to be recognised alongside Facundo Armas, Joe Romm, •Shep Hyken, Vincent Ruinet, Philipp Petry, Dr. Niladri Choudhuri, Aparna K., Monica Sanders, and Vilas Dhar. The future of AI will ultimately be defined not by how intelligent our systems become, but by whether they advance sustainable development for everyone, everywhere.

🌍 Can countries industrialise alone in an era of fragmented markets and global competition?

For many developing economies, the answer is increasingly no.

In Working Paper 96, Baptiste Albertone and Amir Lebdioui argue that #industrialpolicy must move beyond the national scale. Rather than countries competing for the same investment, duplicating industries, or racing to the bottom, they propose a new framework for regional #coordination of industrial policy.

The paper introduces coordinative optimisation, a model in which countries retain full sovereignty while #coordinating investment, productive #specialisation , and regional #value #chains through a shared information and coordination mechanism.

Drawing lessons from ASEAN Foundation , Airbus , and the #EuropeanUnion , the paper argues that successful regional cooperation depends not on deeper supranational governance, but on #trust , #flexibility , and mutually beneficial coordination.

📚 Whether you're a policymaker, researcher, regional organisation, or development practitioner, this paper offers a new perspective on how countries can work together to strengthen industrial capabilities, build regional value chains, and seize green industrialisation opportunities.

Can we truly call an energy system sustainable if it eventually becomes a waste system?

This thought-provoking question was posed by Mr Riad Meddeb, Head of Decarbonization and Sustainable Energy at UNDP, during the #HLPF2026 side event: "Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa"

Held at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, the session was co-organised by Circular Economy Powered Renewable Energy Centre - CEPREC, Chatham House, UNDP, Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE), African Circular Economy Alliance (ACEA), African Development Bank Group and De Montfort University.

The session brought together Member State representatives, UN agencies, regional bodies, researchers, development partners and civil society actors to examine how circular renewable energy systems can support Africa’s clean energy transition.

The discussion moved beyond renewable energy deployment alone. It asked a deeper question: how can Africa expand energy access while avoiding future waste, dependency, affordability challenges and missed opportunities for local value creation?

The session was chaired by Professor Muyiwa Oyinlola, CEPREC Director and Professor of Innovation for Sustainable Development at De Montfort University, with opening framing from Mr Riad Meddeb of UNDP. It featured contributions from representatives of the Permanent Missions of South Africa, Sierra Leone, China and Nigeria to the United Nations, the African Circular Economy Alliance (ACEA), Chatham House Environment and Society, University of Warwick - Warwick Business School, the University of Lagos, ENERGIA Network, UNDP Planet Hub, the SDG7 Youth Constituency, and other partners working across energy, circular economy, policy and implementation.

Key themes included circular design, local value chains for repair and reuse, second-life batteries, standards and e-waste governance, digital tools for transparency and trust, lifecycle finance, and stronger participation by women, young people, informal workers and local enterprises.

The conversation also highlighted the importance of connecting SDG 7 with SDG 8, SDG 9, SDG 11, SDG 12, SDG 13 and SDG 17, while aligning circular renewable energy systems with Africa’s longer-term development vision under Agenda 2063.

For CEPREC, the discussion speaks directly to our mission: generating evidence, building capacity and supporting implementation pathways for circular renewable energy systems across Africa.

Africa’s energy transition must not only deploy more renewable technologies.

It must create systems that deliver access, resilience, jobs, inclusion, local value creation and long-term sustainability.

Thank you to all speakers, partners and participants who contributed to such a rich and timely discussion.
